title: Antenna Height for Distance Calculator
description: Find the antenna height a radio link distance needs with the Antenna Height for Distance Calculator — 4/3-Earth radio horizon maths. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 40 km link to a 10-metre antenna needs about 43 metres of height at your end — the square-root law of the radio horizon, which this calculator inverts for tower planning.
quick_answer: The Antenna Height for Distance Calculator inverts the radio-horizon formula: give it the link distance you need and the other antenna's height, and it returns the height your antenna requires. It uses the standard 4/3-Earth refraction model that radio planners start every line-of-sight estimate with.

Coverage promises begin as horizon arithmetic. A 30 m mast sees about 22.6 km of radio horizon; customer antennas add their own — total link reach is the sum of both horizons.
A ship's antenna at 20 m and a shore station at 60 m share a horizon of about 50 km — the honest ceiling on VHF range, whatever the radio's box claims.
'Height is might' in VHF/UHF. The formula prices exactly how much might each extra 10 metres buys — less each time, by the square root.
Doubling range needs four times the height: 13.0 km from 10 m, but 50 km single-ended demands about 147 m. Every radio planner's intuition is this curve — generous at first, brutal later.
Link range is not one horizon but two: your antenna's horizon plus theirs. Two 30 m antennas reach 22.6 + 22.6 ≈ 45.1 km — which is why raising the low end pays twice as fast as raising the high end.

popular_table.intro: Distance to the radio horizon from a single antenna, standard refraction.
popular_table.note: The 4/3 model (effective Earth radius ≈ 8,495 km) accounts for normal atmospheric refraction bending VHF/UHF waves slightly earthward. Ducting and tropospheric events can extend range far beyond it — weather, not geometry.

faq: What model converts height to distance?
The radio-horizon formula d ≈ 4.12 × √h kilometres (h in metres) under the 4/3-Earth model. Inverting it — h = (d ÷ 4.12)² — is this calculator's direction.

Standard refraction bends radio rays toward the Earth as if the planet were 4/3 its size and the rays straight. It is an engineering convention that matches typical conditions — not a promise about any given day.
Fresnel clearance — height is not enough?

Correct: a working link wants the first Fresnel zone substantially clear (about 60% is the field rule), adding clearance height above obstacles beyond bare horizon math. The Fresnel Zone Calculator on this site sizes that bubble.
The geometric horizon is frequency-blind; higher bands suffer more from obstacles and rain, lower bands bend a little more. The formula is the shared starting geometry for all of them.
Horizon math assumes a smooth Earth (or sea). Hills, buildings and trees subtract — a line-of-sight profile check follows this estimate in real planning.
What if the other antenna's height is zero?
Then your antenna must cover the whole distance alone: height = (distance ÷ 4.12)², the single-ended case in the examples.
